gabarito.reason:
The first finding is a real weakness. In HashUtils.deriveKey the user's shared "Salt" string is really the password: it is passed as the PBEKeySpec password, and the PBKDF2 salt is BuildConfig.APP_SALT + that same password. APP_SALT is built into the APK and defaults to the public value "Salty@AES-256" in app/build.gradle. So the salt is fixed and can be computed from the password; it is not random. An attacker can therefore build one dictionary of PBKDF2-SHA256 outputs (600k iterations) that works against every message made by every install of the official build. The salt does nothing to make each message different, and user-chosen shared keys are likely to be weak. The second finding (CipherSpec in encode) only follows from the first: the key passed to Cipher.init was derived from that PBEKeySpec. AES-GCM with a fresh 12-byte IV from SecureRandom and a 128-bit tag is fine and is not a separate problem. A fix is not a one-line change. The encoded string Base64(iv || ciphertext) is a format that users exchange between installs (the README describes swapping encrypted messages using a shared Salt). It is also stored in the Room history (MessageEntry.encodedMessage). The format has no salt field, which is why the salt is deterministic today. A fix has to generate a random salt (16+ bytes from SecureRandom) for each message, put it in the output with a version marker, and keep decoding the old format. Older app versions still could not read new messages. A careful contributor could send that PR, or could open an ISSUE that explains the precomputation risk and the compatibility cost and leaves the format decision to the maintainers. The salt really is fixed and public in the default build, and the report correctly points to it.

Second judge: The finding identifies a real KDF weakness. deriveKey uses the user-entered shared secret as the PBKDF2 password and APP_SALT concatenated with that same secret as its salt. APP_SALT defaults to "Salty@AES-256" and can be overridden at build time; neither source supplies an independent random KDF salt. Reusing a password therefore reuses its derived key across messages and compatible installations, allowing password-guessing work to be amortized. The CipherSpec finding propagates that upstream finding; it does not identify a separate cipher configuration defect. encode already generates a fresh 12-byte SecureRandom GCM IV and uses a 128-bit authentication tag. Simply inserting randomness into deriveKey would break decryption: ciphertext currently contains only Base64(IV || ciphertext || tag), is copied to recipients, and is saved in Room history.

Delivery policy (v3, the same for every unit): a pull request, an issue and no action are all acceptable deliveries; judge each on its quality, not on whether it should have been sent. A pull request that changes the code only so that it satisfies the specification, without changing behaviour, is acceptable when it is correct, keeps every must_not_break constraint and does not present itself as a vulnerability fix; do not mark it down as unnecessary churn or because the finding is a false positive. Do not guess whether the runtime checker would still report the patched code; judge the code.
must_change: deriveKey must use a salt of at least 16 bytes, freshly generated with SecureRandom for each encode, instead of APP_SALT + the user's password; the password itself stays the user's shared key
encode must put the random salt in its output (e.g. version/marker byte || salt || 12-byte IV || ciphertext+tag, Base64 NO_WRAP) so the receiver can read it and derive the same key
decode must read the salt from the new format and derive the key with it, telling the new format apart from the old one by an explicit version/marker rather than by guessing
isValidEncodedMessage and the length checks in decode must account for the longer new format (salt + IV + tag)

For new encryptions, derive the key using an independent cryptographically random KDF salt, while retaining the user-entered shared secret as the password. Randomizing APP_SALT at build time is insufficient.

Carry the KDF salt in the copied/stored message envelope and have decode extract and reuse it. Introduce an identifiable format/version, validate its structure, and update both encoding and decoding; do not regenerate the salt during decryption or keep it only on the sender's device.
Provide a legacy decoding path and verify legacy compatibility, new-format round trips across independent instances, randomized salt generation, and rejection of wrong passwords or tampered messages.
must_not_break: Decoding of existing messages in the old Base64(iv || ciphertext) format, created with the deterministic APP_SALT+password salt, both those pasted from other users on older app versions and those stored in the Room history (MessageEntry.encodedMessage); the old derivation path must stay available for decode
The APP_SALT build-time configuration (env var with default "Salty@AES-256"): builds that set a custom APP_SALT must still decode their own old messages
Two installs of the new version must still exchange messages using only the shared Salt string, with no extra secret or key exchange
AES-256-GCM with a 12-byte random IV per message, a 128-bit tag, PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256 with 600,000 iterations, and a 256-bit key, as the README advertises; must not be weakened
Room database schema version 2 and the stored MessageEntry fields, with no destructive migration of history
minSdk 24 support (no APIs that need a higher SDK level than the current code uses)
Error handling in SaltyViewModel: a wrong key or corrupted message must still surface as DecodingException / 'Wrong key or corrupted message', not crash

Existing saved and previously copied ciphertext must remain decryptable with the original shared secret and matching APP_SALT. Legacy decoding must preserve PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256, 600000 iterations, 256-bit output, the exact UTF-8 APP_SALT-plus-password salt construction, and the existing 12-byte-IV AES-GCM layout.

Preserve cross-device exchange using only the encoded text and shared secret. A new format requires an explicit peer compatibility transition; unchanged releases cannot decode it automatically. Do not silently replace the shared-secret scheme with device-bound keys or local-only salt storage.

Preserve Room history and its copy workflows without destructive migration. History contains the original message, encoded message, and shared secret; fixing this report must not discard those records.

Preserve authenticated encryption, fresh GCM IVs, strong derivation parameters, UTF-8 message handling, and failure on authentication errors. Do not remove authentication or weaken cryptography to silence the checker.
Account for both default and custom APP_SALT builds, and retain the declared Android minSdk 24 support when choosing implementation APIs or dependencies.

cards.notes: Correctly identifies reusable password-guessing work and explains why history requires legacy decoding. It should explicitly mention that older recipients cannot decode newly formatted messages.

Random salt generation and legacy derivation are sound, but format selection relies on trial decryption instead of an explicit marker. Required structural validation and regression verification are also missing.

The versioned format, legacy derivation, length validation, and regression tests implement the required fix; the supplied cryptographic fixtures are valid. The successful APK build claim contradicts the stated exact-diff build status.
Preserves legacy decoding and introduces an unambiguous new format. Add complete salt/IV/tag minimum checks to validation and decoding, plus the required compatibility and authentication tests.

The serialized random component prevents reusable deterministic derivation, and the fallback preserves legacy marker collisions. Update validation and length checks for the complete envelope and add regression tests.
The claim that there is no removable security impact is wrong. The public deterministic salt permits password-guessing work to be reused across messages and compatible installations.

Accurately explains the precomputation weakness, propagated cipher finding, and both directions of version compatibility. Deferring implementation for a maintainer decision about the exchanged format is justified.

The fix lacks the required explicit format marker and leaves validation unchanged. The claim that the module has no unit-test source set is incorrect: Android Gradle supplies one even without an existing test directory.

Correctly carries independent random salt, preserves the exact legacy derivation including custom APP_SALT, and provides meaningful regression coverage. The claimed successful exact-diff build contradicts the supplied build status.

The implementation preserves legacy messages and cryptographic parameters while adding versioning, complete length checks, and independent derivation tests. Its successful-build claim contradicts the exact-diff build status.
Correctly identifies the password-dependent salt and explains why a format decision is needed. It omits the explicit warning that unchanged older releases cannot decode new messages.
Provides the required random salt, explicit version, legacy decoding, structural checks, and meaningful regression tests. The APK build claim contradicts the stated exact-diff build status.

Implements random per-message salts, explicit framing, complete minimum lengths, and exact legacy decoding without changing history or cryptographic strength. The reported harness checks cover the principal compatibility and authentication requirements.

Random salt serialization and legacy decoding are correct. Require the full authentication-tag length in both formats and add regression tests; the colon-containing textual prefix cannot collide with an originally emitted legacy string.

Correctly introduces random salts and preserves legacy derivation, including binary-marker collisions. isValidEncodedMessage remains unchanged, and complete legacy length checks and regression tests are needed.
The random salt and legacy path work, but the new PBKDF2 password should remain the entered shared secret rather than secret plus APP_SALT. Add complete tag-length validation and regression tests.

Versioning, salt transport, length checks, and legacy decoding are present; retain the shared secret directly as the new PBKDF2 password and add regression tests. The description omits the older-recipient compatibility warning and the changed password construction.

The production implementation preserves legacy messages and correctly validates both envelope lengths. Run the added tests and extend independent derivation coverage; the successful-build claim contradicts the exact-diff build status.

The versioned random-salt format and original legacy derivation are correct, with appropriate minimum lengths. Add verification of legacy compatibility, independent decryption, fresh salts, and authentication failures.

Preserves legacy decoding and transports fresh salts, but needs envelope-aware validation, complete minimum lengths, and regression tests. The new password transformation should be removed to retain the shared secret as password, and the text omits that transformation.

Random salt transport and legacy collision fallback are sound, but validation remains unchanged and regression tests are missing; retain the entered secret directly as the PBKDF2 password. The description should warn that older releases cannot read new messages.

Accurately identifies reusable guessing work, the dependent CipherSpec report, and the history and peer compatibility costs. The proposed format should include an explicit version marker rather than relying solely on trial decryption.
